query: FeCoNi is an fcc alloy with high saturation magnetization and a low coercive field. Earlier studies examined the high-entropy alloys FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt, but both exhibited soft ferromagnetism. A qualifying high-entropy alloy must have an almost equiatomic multicomponent composition and configurational entropy of at least 1.0R. Subject to these constraints, what single intervention could produce a FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy with greater coercivity than the prior derivatives? Present one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an appropriate FeCoNi-based baseline, defines the conditions over which it should apply, cites supporting observations from earlier work, and proposes a discriminating experiment with an explicit falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: A rapid thermal annealing (RTA) procedure tuned to promote grain refinement in an equiatomic FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy will raise the coercivity compared to conventionally processed FeCoNi alloys (and the previously explored FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt derivatives) by increasing domain wall pinning despite retaining high saturation magnetization.
generation.material_initial_state: An equiatomic FeCoNi high-entropy alloy produced by conventional processing that results in a coarse-grained, single-phase FCC structure with high saturation magnetization and low coercivity.
generation.intervention: Implement a modified RTA treatment—specifically lowering the annealing temperature and shortening the dwell time—to refine the grain structure and induce local strains while preserving the overall FCC phase and high configurational entropy.
generation.conditions: Conduct RTA in an inert atmosphere (e.g., argon) at approximately 600°C for around 15 minutes (or other optimized time/temperature conditions) rather than a higher temperature/longer annealing cycle used as baseline, ensuring the processing window maintains a single-phase structure.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries produced by a reduced grain size act as effective domain wall pinning centers; the increased density of these boundaries (and any strain-induced local anisotropy) enhances the coercivity of the alloy.
generation.mechanism: By refining the grain size, more grain boundaries are formed, which act as pinning sites that impede domain wall motion. This microstructural change increases magnetocrystalline anisotropy locally due to strain and possible minute compositional fluctuations at the boundaries, resulting in higher coercivity despite the overall high saturation magnetization of the FCC FeCoNi phase.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified RTA treatment should substantially increase the coercive field relative to the baseline FeCoNi alloy while maintaining a high saturation magnetization, thereby rendering the material a harder magnet compared to the previously reported soft ferromagnetic FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt derivatives.
generation.baseline: FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloys produced by conventional processing (or by the earlier Pt- or Pd-addition routes) that yield a coarse-grained, highly symmetric FCC structure exhibiting low coercivity.
generation.boundary: The coercivity enhancement is expected as long as the material remains a single-phase FCC high-entropy alloy with equiatomic composition and does not undergo unwanted phase decompositions or excessive ordering that might reduce the saturation magnetization.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the coercivity increase is uncertain; it depends on the degree of grain refinement and the stability of the induced microstructure. Additionally, careful optimization is required to avoid degradation of other magnetic properties.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a set of equiatomic FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy samples using identical melting and mixing procedures. Divide them into groups subjected to different RTA parameters: a baseline treatment (e.g., high temperature such as 1000°C for 15 h) versus varying lower temperatures (e.g., 600°C) and shorter dwell times (e.g., 15 min). Utilize transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) to quantify grain size and confirm phase purity. Measure the magnetic properties (coercivity and saturation magnetization) with a vibrating sample magnetometer (VSM) at room temperature.
measurements: Magnetic hysteresis loops to extract coercivity (Hc) and saturation magnetization (Ms)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the RTA-treated samples with finer grains do not show a statistically significant increase in coercivity compared to the baseline sample (or if any gain in coercivity is accompanied by a detrimental decrease in saturation magnetization), then the hypothesis that grain refinement via modified RTA enhances coercivity is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Therefore, the bimodal coercivity distribution observed in the OOP direction is explained by a 2‐step process of magnetization reversal beginning with easy domain nucleation and propagation in the large (001) oriented grains (narrow low Hc peak), followed by pinning between grains with small size and varying easy‐axis direction (broad high Hc peak). The distribution of size and easy‐axis orientation both manifest in the spreading of the high Hc peak along the Hc axis. Based on this, we expect that the Hc could be enhanced through microstructural optimization such as a reduction in grain size, which may be achieved by adjusting the RTA time and temperature.
